Week 6 — Economic Dashboards and Data Storytelling

Week 4 prepared the data.

Week 5 generated evidence.

Week 6 communicates the evidence.

The central question is:

How can we turn economic analysis into a dashboard that supports understanding and decision-making?

This week is not about decoration. It is about analytical communication.

1. Connection to Weeks 1-5

Week 6 integrates the course so far.

Previous Week Skill Used in Week 6
Week 1 Running Python and interpreting outputs
Week 2 Understanding observations, variables, and data
Week 3 Applying rules and logic
Week 4 Preparing analysis-ready data
Week 5 Creating evidence and interpretation

The workflow is:

Prepared data -> Evidence -> Dashboard -> Story

2. Learning Outcomes

By the end of this week, students should be able to:

  • explain the purpose of an economic dashboard
  • identify the audience and analytical question for a dashboard
  • select charts based on analytical purpose
  • build interactive Plotly line, bar, and scatter charts
  • add hover information and readable titles
  • combine several indicators into a multi-panel dashboard
  • evaluate dashboard design quality
  • write a dashboard story using claim, evidence, meaning, and caution
  • avoid decorative or misleading dashboards

5. Why Dashboards Matter in Economics

Economists often communicate with people who need quick, reliable insight:

  • policymakers
  • researchers
  • businesses
  • journalists
  • students
  • the public

A dashboard helps users see:

  • what changed
  • when it changed
  • which indicators moved together
  • where warning signs appeared
  • what needs further investigation

A dashboard is not:

many graphs placed on one page

A dashboard is:

a guided analytical view of an economic problem

6. Define the Dashboard Before Coding

Before writing code, answer six design questions:

  1. Who is the audience?
  2. What question should the dashboard answer?
  3. Which indicators matter most?
  4. Which chart type fits each indicator?
  5. What should the reader notice first?
  6. What caution should accompany the dashboard?

For this course, the dashboard question is:

How did Sri Lanka's macroeconomic conditions change across the period?

7. Chart Selection

Analytical Question Best Chart
How did inflation change over time? Line chart
Which years had negative GDP growth? Bar chart with zero reference
Did inflation and exchange rate change move together? Scatter plot
Which year shows multiple stress signals? Evidence table or dashboard summary
What is the main story? Multi-panel dashboard

Chart choice should follow analytical purpose.

Do not choose charts because they look impressive.

8. Load Data and Prepared Variables

import pandas as pd
import plotly.express as px
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots
import plotly.graph_objects as go

url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kanishkawerawella/ECN4199_Website/main/data/sri_lanka_macro.csv"
data = pd.read_csv(url)

data["Exchange_Rate_Change"] = data["Exchange_Rate"].pct_change() * 100
data["Recession"] = data["GDP_Growth"] < 0
data["Low_Reserves"] = data["Reserves"] < 4000

Inflation category:

def classify_inflation(rate):
    if rate < 5:
        return "Low"
    elif rate <= 15:
        return "Moderate"
    else:
        return "High"

data["Inflation_Category"] = data["Inflation"].apply(classify_inflation)

9. Interactive Line Chart

fig = px.line(
    data,
    x="Year",
    y="Inflation",
    markers=True,
    title="Inflation Over Time",
    hover_data=["GDP_Growth", "Exchange_Rate", "Reserves"]
)

fig.show()

Teaching point:

Hover information allows users to inspect context without overcrowding the chart.

Ask:

  • What year should the reader notice first?
  • What other values help explain that year?

10. Interactive Bar Chart

fig = px.bar(
    data,
    x="Year",
    y="GDP_Growth",
    color="Recession",
    title="GDP Growth and Recession Years"
)

fig.show()

Interpretation:

The bar chart separates years of expansion from years of contraction.

Design question:

Does color help interpretation, or does it distract?

11. Interactive Scatter Plot

fig = px.scatter(
    data,
    x="Inflation",
    y="Exchange_Rate_Change",
    hover_name="Year",
    size="Unemployment",
    color="Inflation_Category",
    title="Inflation and Exchange Rate Change"
)

fig.show()

This chart allows users to inspect:

  • relationship between inflation and exchange rate change
  • crisis years
  • inflation category
  • unemployment context

Reminder:

This chart suggests association, not causation.

12. Dashboard Summary Indicators

Before building charts, create simple summary values.

highest_inflation_year = data.loc[data["Inflation"].idxmax(), "Year"]
lowest_growth_year = data.loc[data["GDP_Growth"].idxmin(), "Year"]
lowest_reserves_year = data.loc[data["Reserves"].idxmin(), "Year"]

highest_inflation_year, lowest_growth_year, lowest_reserves_year

These values help identify what the dashboard should highlight.

13. Multi-Panel Monitoring Dashboard

fig = make_subplots(
    rows=3,
    cols=1,
    subplot_titles=(
        "Inflation",
        "GDP Growth",
        "Exchange Rate"
    )
)

fig.add_trace(
    go.Scatter(x=data["Year"], y=data["Inflation"], mode="lines+markers", name="Inflation"),
    row=1,
    col=1
)

fig.add_trace(
    go.Bar(x=data["Year"], y=data["GDP_Growth"], name="GDP Growth"),
    row=2,
    col=1
)

fig.add_trace(
    go.Scatter(x=data["Year"], y=data["Exchange_Rate"], mode="lines+markers", name="Exchange Rate"),
    row=3,
    col=1
)

fig.update_layout(
    height=850,
    title_text="Macroeconomic Monitoring Dashboard",
    showlegend=False
)

fig.show()

This dashboard shows price instability, output contraction, and exchange rate movement together.

14. Improving Dashboard Design

Good dashboards are:

  • focused
  • readable
  • consistent
  • clearly labelled
  • connected to a question
  • supported by interpretation

Weak dashboards often have:

  • too many charts
  • unclear titles
  • missing units
  • random colors
  • no main story
  • no caution about limitations

Design principle:

Every chart must earn its place.

15. Dashboard Storytelling

A dashboard should be accompanied by a short story.

Use this structure:

Part Purpose
Claim State the main pattern
Evidence Refer to values or charts
Meaning Explain why it matters economically
Caution State what the dashboard cannot prove

Example:

The dashboard suggests that 2022 was the strongest macroeconomic stress point in the period. Inflation reached 46.4 percent while GDP growth was -7.8 percent and the exchange rate increased sharply. This combination signals pressure on prices, output, and external stability. However, the dashboard is descriptive and should not be interpreted as a causal model.

16. Dashboard Design Review

Students should review their dashboard using this checklist:

  1. Is the main question clear?
  2. Are the most important indicators visible?
  3. Are titles and labels understandable?
  4. Does color help interpretation?
  5. Can the reader identify the key year or pattern quickly?
  6. Is there a written interpretation?
  7. Is there a caution about what cannot be concluded?

18. Mini Quiz

Question 1

What is the main purpose of a dashboard?

Correct answer:

To organize and communicate evidence for understanding or decision-making.

Question 2

Should dashboards include as many charts as possible?

Correct answer:

No. Dashboards should include only charts that support the analytical question.

Question 3

What is the danger of an interactive chart without interpretation?

Correct answer:

Users may explore the chart but miss the economic meaning or overstate the conclusion.

19. Common Student Mistakes

Mistake Why It Is a Problem
Creating decorative charts Distracts from analysis
Using too many colors Makes the dashboard confusing
Missing titles and labels Reduces readability
Not linking charts to a question Produces disconnected visuals
Claiming causation from dashboard patterns Overstates descriptive evidence
Forgetting a written story Leaves the dashboard without interpretation

20. Responsible AI Use in Week 6

AI tools can help with Plotly syntax, but students must control the analytical story.

Good AI prompt:

Help me improve the readability of a Plotly dashboard that shows inflation, GDP growth, and exchange rate trends. Do not change my economic interpretation.

Weak AI prompt:

Make a dashboard and explain everything.

Students must verify:

  • the variables used
  • the chart types
  • labels and units
  • the evidence in the story
  • the caution statement

21. Week 6 Output

By the end of the two-hour lecture, students should have:

  • one dashboard question
  • three interactive charts
  • one multi-panel dashboard
  • one design review
  • one dashboard story
  • one caution about interpretation

22. Closing Message

The main lesson of Week 6 is:

Economic analysis becomes valuable when it is communicated clearly, honestly, and usefully.

Students should now be able to move through a complete applied workflow:

prepare data -> analyze evidence -> communicate findings
